catalog_quote: The basic patterns of stress in Warlmanpa are: a) disyllabic morphemes (including roots) receive stress on their initial syllable; b) adjacent syllables cannot both be stressed; and c) word-final syllables cannot be stressed. ... Stress assignment is determined by the position of the syllable in the phonological and prosodic word. Syllables are assigned to feet, where each disyllable in a prosodic word constitutes a well-formed foot, from first to last ... Any remaining unassigned syllables are then linked to the same foot as the preceding syllable. ... A syllable that does not have any weak branches up to the phonological word receives primary stress (this is always, and only, the initial syllable of a phonological word, with a single known exception: mayi'patturla); all other strong syllables receive secondary stress. audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed initial primary stress, weight-blind, trochaic secondary stress with prosodic-word restart at polysyllabic suffixes, one listed lexical exception) rests on a 2024 open-access ANU reference grammar whose stress section we hold and whose deciding quotation I confirmed verbatim at sec. 2.6.1 pp. 50-52 incl. fn. 4. Glottolog's only grammar ref is the 2021 thesis this book supersedes; Nash's exhaustive Warlmanpa bibliography (Dec 2025) lists no stress/prosody study. The sole earlier primary source, Nash 1979 sec. 14B, was downloaded and agrees. Nothing better exists; no reclassification or grade change needed. One caveat already carried by the source itself (fn. 4: mora-sensitivity not investigated) does not affect the fixed: initial syllable primary-stress coding. downloaded files and record:

sources.citation: Nash, David G. 1979 [rev. 1981, online version last changed 16 Sep 2020]. Grammatical Preface to Vocabulary of the Warlmanpa Language. www0.anu.edu.au/linguistics/nash/aust/wpa/
sources.quote: 'B. Stress falls on the first syllable of each word. There is a secondary stress on the first syllable (and third syllable of a four syllable morpheme) of a morpheme of two or more syllables. Adjacent monosyllabic morphemes received an alternating secondary stress, but not so as to produce two adjacent stresses or a word-final stress.'
sources.locator: sec. (14) Phonological rules, item B (unpaginated HTML; the text)
sources.note: Only independent primary stress statement predating Browne; Browne 2024 says his stress account 'largely follows Nash 1979'. downloaded now; confirms initial primary stress, no adjacent stresses, no word-final stress.
